paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Limestone is a carbonate sedimentary rock and the main source of the material lime. It is made mostly of calcite and aragonite, two minerals that are different crystal forms of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃. Carbonate rock makes up about 20% to 25% of sedimentary rock, and most of that is limestone. The rest is mostly dolomite, a closely related rock.

paragraphs.heading: How it forms
paragraphs.text: Limestone forms when calcite and aragonite precipitate out of water that holds dissolved calcium. Both biological and nonbiological processes can do this. Biological ones, such as corals and shells piling up in the sea, have likely mattered more over the last 540 million years. Most limestone formed in shallow marine settings such as continental shelves or platforms, with smaller amounts formed in many other environments.

paragraphs.heading: The grains inside
paragraphs.text: Most limestone is sand-sized grains set in a matrix of carbonate mud. Most of those grains are bits of skeleton from marine organisms, coral or foraminifera for example. These organisms secrete structures of aragonite or calcite and leave them behind when they die. Other grains are ooids: sand-sized grains in which a central quartz grain or carbonate mineral fragment is wrapped in one or more layers of calcite or aragonite. Ooids likely form when calcium carbonate precipitates directly onto them.

paragraphs.heading: What the grains record
paragraphs.text: Limestone often contains fossils, which tell scientists about ancient environments and the evolution of life. Skeletal grains have a composition that reflects the organisms that made them and the environment where they were made. Coral grains, for example, are more common in high-energy environments, with strong currents and turbulence. Bryozoan grains are more common in low-energy environments, where the water is quiet.

paragraphs.heading: Color, pores and strength
paragraphs.text: Limestone is commonly white to gray. Limestone unusually rich in organic matter can be almost black, and traces of iron or manganese can turn it off-white to yellow to red. Its porosity runs from 0.1% in the densest limestone to 40% in chalk. Limestone is fairly soft, scoring 2 to 4 on the Mohs hardness scale, yet the crushing strength of dense limestone can reach 180 MPa. Concrete, for comparison, typically has a crushing strength of about 40 MPa.

paragraphs.heading: Caves and uses
paragraphs.text: Limestone is exposed over large regions of Earth's surface. It is slightly soluble in rainwater, so these exposures often erode into karst landscapes, and most cave systems are found in limestone bedrock. It also has many uses: as a feedstock for the lime used in cement, as aggregate under roads, as a white pigment or filler in toothpaste, paint and similar products, and as a soil conditioner. About 30% of the world's petroleum reservoirs lie in limestone formations.
